finding.suggestionContent: `start` and `end` are counted independently over `value` and `sanitized`, which can have different lengths, and nothing guarantees `start + end <= value.length()`. When `sanitized` is longer than `value` (the sanitizer inserts `<!-- -->` markers and only the exact literal `"<!-- -->"` is stripped) or when multiple edits leave matching prefix and suffix regions, `start` can exceed `value.length() - end`, so `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` and aborts verification instead of reporting the difference. Clamp the indices (e.g. compute `end = Math.min(end, value.length() - start)` and the same for `sanitized`) before slicing.

Because `tagDeviceUI` returns early on a cache hit (line 84), every subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute TTL returns `nil`, so `TagDevice` succeeds and `Authenticate` (client.go:44) issues an anonymous identity — the device limit is silently bypassed for that device for ~29 minutes after its first rejection. finding.suggestionContent: `Authenticate` now calls `TagDevice` synchronously, whereas the removed goroutine previously tagged devices off the request path with a 2-minute timeout. `TagDevice` executes `CountDevices` (SELECT COUNT) plus `CreateOrUpdateDevice` (INSERT/UPDATE) inline, so every anonymous authentication request now blocks on two database round-trips before the identity is returned, adding latency and DB load on the auth hot path for all anonymous users. If the synchronous call is required to enforce the limit, avoid the extra `CountDevices` query on the common path (e.g. rely on the conditional UPDATE/INSERT to detect the limit) or keep the tagging non-blocking for the non-limit case.

finding.suggestionContent: The limit check (`CountDevices` then INSERT) is not atomic: two concurrent anonymous requests with different device IDs can both read `count < s.deviceLimit` and both insert, so a burst of parallel requests registers more devices than the configured limit. The INSERT's `ON CONFLICT (device_id)` only dedupes the same device, not the total count, and no transaction or lock serializes the check against the write. Enforce the limit atomically, e.g. perform the count and insert in a single transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or gate the write behind a server lock.

finding.suggestionContent: The write lock is taken without re-checking entryPointAssetsCache, so every goroutine that saw nil on the fast path serializes on Lock() and each performs a full os.Open + JSON decode of assets-manifest.json while holding the exclusive lock. On a cold cache at startup this amplifies one file read into N (N = concurrent requests), and all other readers block on RLock for the duration of the blocking disk I/O — a regression versus the previous lock-free behavior. After acquiring the write lock, re-check the cache and return the already-populated value if present, e.g. `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after line 48, and prefer loading the manifest outside the lock.

finding.suggestionContent: The `for` loop over `self.processes` calls `break` when the deadline has passed, so any process that appears after the first one in the dict is never waited on nor `terminate()`d. With `max_processes > 1` those flusher processes are left running after `join()` returns. Change the `break` to continue terminating the remaining processes (or terminate in a `finally`).

finding.suggestionContent: `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` yields 0 when `assigned_shards` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` and `self.processes` empty. `_ensure_processes_alive` then iterates nothing and `submit()` never flushes, so the consumer silently processes and commits offsets while writing nothing to Kafka. Guard against an empty shard list (raise or assert `num_processes >= 1`).

finding.label: performance
finding.suggestionContent: submit() now calls get_memory_info() once per flusher process and concatenates the results, but get_memory_info() returns the FULL Redis cluster INFO for every master node and does not filter by the buffer's assigned_shards, so all buffers return identical data. This multiplies the Redis INFO round-trips by num_processes on every submit and builds an N-times-duplicated list of the same nodes. Call get_memory_info() once (e.g. from a single shared buffer/client) instead of iterating self.buffers.
